title: Aplatanado — the island pace
body: The single word that explains daily life here. Aplatanado (literally 'gone all banana-y') is the unhurried Canarian rhythm — calm, never in a rush, 'we'll get to it'. It's not laziness; it's a deliberate refusal to be stressed. Once you slow to island time — long lunches, late evenings outside, nobody hurrying you — you start to feel it too.

title: Magua — the bittersweet word
body: A word that exists only here. Magua isn't quite nostalgia or sadness — it's the specific sweet ache of something good ending: the last evening of a trip, a sunset fading, a goodbye. Canarian emigrants who left for the Americas built whole songs and poems around it. There's even a saying: 'Más vale magua que dolor' — better the regret of having tried than the pain of never having.

title: Sobremesa — the meal isn't the point
body: The sacred lingering after a meal, when the plates are cleared but nobody leaves — drinks topped up, the conversation just getting good. A Canarian doesn't eat and run; the food was just the excuse to sit together. If a local invites you to lunch, clear your afternoon.

title: Papas, mojo & gofio — the island on a plate
body: Three things tell you you're really in the Canaries. Papas arrugadas — little potatoes boiled to wrinkling in heavy salt (once in seawater, because fresh water was scarce). Mojo — the punchy sauces, red (paprika/chilli) and green (coriander), that go on everything. And gofio — toasted milled grain the Guanches ate before the Spanish ever arrived, still on the table today: a literal, edible thread back to the island's first people.

title: The Guanches — the island's first people
body: Before the Spanish conquest, Tenerife was home to the Guanches — a tall, fair, cave-dwelling people related to the Berbers of North Africa, who mummified their dead and worshipped Mount Teide. They were never fully erased, only mixed in: their blood, their words, their gofio and their myths (like Guayota, the demon in the volcano) survive in today's islanders. The name Dácil, a Guanche princess, is still given to girls here.

title: Why Canarian Spanish sounds Caribbean
body: Listen closely and the Spanish here sounds more like Cuba than Madrid — soft, melodic, with 'ustedes' instead of 'vosotros' and seseo (c and z said as s). That's no accident: for centuries Canarians emigrated to Cuba and Venezuela and came back, carrying the accent home. It's also why a bus is a guagua here, not an autobús, and why the food and music carry a Latin-American warmth.

title: What Canarians are like
body: Ask a local to describe themselves and you'll hear the same words: amable, tranquilo, hospitalario, cercano — kind, calm, hospitable, close. Centuries on the edge of empire, between Europe, Africa and the Americas, bred an open, easy-going, conflict-smoothing people who treat a stranger like a guest. Understated rather than boastful — they'd rather the island do the bragging.

title: Carnaval — the island lets loose
body: Once a year the calm cracks wide open: the Carnaval of Santa Cruz is one of the biggest in the world, rivalled only by Rio. Weeks of costumes, drag galas, all-night street parties (verbenas) and a mock 'burial of the sardine' to end it. It's the aplatanado island's other face — proof that under the calm, Canarians know exactly how to throw a party.
